q.s: A 58-year-old woman has had two kidney stones in a year, constipation, fatigue and low mood. She takes no supplements or diuretics. Serum phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase is mildly elevated and creatinine is normal. 24-hour urine calcium is high. Her serum calcium and intact PTH are plotted on the nomogram shown.
o: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease
e: Wrong. PTH suppressed, alkalosis, renal failure.
Wrong. Intact PTH would be suppressed.
Wrong. PTH would be suppressed.
Wrong. Urine calcium would be low.
Correct. High calcium with inappropriately high PTH, low phosphate and hypercalciuria is primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single adenoma.
Wrong. Calcium would be low or normal, phosphate high, creatinine abnormal.
Wrong. Calcitriol-mediated, PTH suppressed.
cl: two kidney stones in a year, constipation, fatigue and low mood
She takes no supplements or diuretics
Excludes calcium/vitamin D excess and thiazides.
q.ch: Hypercalcemia + high PTH (plot) + low phosphate + hypercalciuria + normal kidneys → primary hyperparathyroidism → adenoma.
q.tr: High Ca with a "not-low" PTH = parathyroid problem; high Ca with low PTH = everything else.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

q.s: A 36-year-old man has had polyuria (8 L/day) and intense thirst since undergoing transsphenoidal resection of a craniopharyngioma 1 week ago. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L. A supervised water deprivation test is performed; the results are shown.
e: Wrong. Used for nephrogenic DI.
Wrong. Treats primary polydipsia; dangerous here.
Correct. Failure to concentrate urine with deprivation but a >50% rise after desmopressin indicates central DI; replace ADH with desmopressin.
Wrong. An ADH antagonist for SIADH.
Wrong. Causes nephrogenic DI.
Wrong. Used for SIADH.
cl: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary.
q.ch: Pituitary surgery + polyuria + hypernatremia + no rise in urine osmolality with deprivation + large rise after desmopressin → central DI → desmopressin.
q.tr: Desmopressin "Delivers" in central DI; in nephrogenic DI it "Doesn't."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

q.s: A 59-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history has rapidly progressive weakness, edema, hypertension and darkening of his skin over 2 months. Serum K+ is 2.6 mEq/L and glucose is 260 mg/dL. He has no striae or central obesity. Endocrine test results are shown.
e: Wrong. Not indicated.
Correct. ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome that does not suppress and does not respond to CRH suggests ectopic ACTH, classically small cell lung cancer in a smoker.
Wrong. ACTH is high, so the source is not adrenal.
Wrong. A pituitary source would usually suppress with high-dose dexamethasone and respond to CRH.
Wrong. He already has cortisol excess.
Wrong. Find the source first.
cl: Risk factor for small cell lung cancer.
rapidly progressive weakness, edema, hypertension and darkening of his skin
Very high ACTH and cortisol develop quickly; MSH-like pigmentation.
He has no striae or central obesity
Too rapid for classic Cushingoid features.
q.ch: Smoker + rapid hypercortisolism with hypokalemia and pigmentation + very high ACTH + no suppression, no CRH response → ectopic ACTH → small cell lung cancer → CT chest.
q.tr: High ACTH: "pituitary listens (suppresses with high-dose dex, responds to CRH), ectopic ignores."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

head: Test
Result
rows: No rise in ACTH or cortisol

q.s: A 26-year-old nurse has had palpitations, heat intolerance and a 7-kg weight loss for 2 months. Pulse is 112/min. The thyroid is not enlarged or tender. There is no exophthalmos. Her test results are shown.
e: Wrong. Painful gland, high ESR and high thyroglobulin.
Wrong. Low uptake, but thyroglobulin is high from gland destruction.
Wrong. Nodular gland with patchy high uptake.
Wrong. RAIU would be high and diffuse.
Wrong. Low neck uptake but thyroglobulin is not suppressed.
Correct. Thyrotoxicosis with low iodine uptake and low thyroglobulin means hormone is coming from outside the gland; the gland is suppressed.
cl: Health worker with access to medications.
The thyroid is not enlarged or tender
Not Graves goiter or painful thyroiditis.
q.ch: Thyrotoxicosis + low RAIU (gland not making hormone) + low thyroglobulin (gland not releasing stored hormone) → exogenous thyroid hormone.
q.tr: Low uptake + low thyroglobulin = "Took it" (pills); low uptake + high thyroglobulin = "Torn" gland (thyroiditis).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated after her father and aunt developed thyroid cancer. Her family pedigree is shown (she is the arrow, III-2; shaded symbols indicate medullary thyroid carcinoma; the aunt II-4 also had episodic hypertension from an adrenal tumor). Her serum calcitonin is mildly elevated.
e: Correct. Autosomal dominant medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma is MEN2 (RET proto-oncogene); carriers need prophylactic thyroidectomy.
Wrong. Somatic mutation in papillary carcinoma.
Wrong. Familial adenomatous polyposis.
Wrong. Not associated with medullary carcinoma.
Wrong. MEN1 does not include medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Wrong. VHL causes pheochromocytoma but not medullary carcinoma.
cl: father and aunt developed thyroid cancer
episodic hypertension from an adrenal tumor
C-cell hyperplasia or early medullary carcinoma.
q.ch: Vertical transmission (autosomal dominant) of medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma → MEN2 → RET mutation → prophylactic thyroidectomy.
q.tr: "RET = REmove Thyroid."
q.q2: A germline mutation in which gene is most likely, and what is the recommended management for carriers?

q.s: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes injects insulin twice daily. He wakes at 3 AM sweating and shaky several times a week; fingerstick glucose is 48 mg/dL at those times. His morning glucose is then 240 mg/dL. Plasma insulin profiles after a subcutaneous dose of three preparations are shown; he takes curve 2 at 10 PM.
e: Wrong. Long acting with a flat profile (curve 3).
Wrong. Very long acting, flat.
Wrong. Short acting: peaks at 2–4 hours.
Correct. Intermediate-acting NPH peaks about 4–10 hours after injection; a bedtime dose peaks around 2–4 AM, causing nocturnal hypoglycemia (and rebound morning hyperglycemia, the Somogyi effect).
Wrong. Long acting.
Wrong. Rapid acting (curve 1): peaks within 1 hour.
cl: wakes at 3 AM sweating and shaky
q.ch: Bedtime intermediate insulin peaking at 4–6 h → 2–4 AM hypoglycemia → counter-regulatory rebound → high fasting glucose → curve 2 is NPH (fix: move NPH earlier or switch to glargine).
q.tr: Insulin "speeds": Lispro = sprint (1 h), Regular = jog, NPH = hill (peak 6 h), Glargine = flat road.
q.q2: Which insulin does curve 2 represent?
q.fc: Plasma insulin profiles of three preparations

q.s: In a physiology experiment, healthy volunteers receive glucose either orally or as an intravenous infusion adjusted so that plasma glucose concentrations are identical in both conditions. Plasma insulin responses are shown.
e: Wrong. Reduces hepatic glucose output.
Wrong. Slows carbohydrate absorption.
Wrong. Acts directly on β-cell K+ channels regardless of route.
Wrong. Increases insulin sensitivity.
Correct. The incretin effect: gut hormones (GLP-1 from L cells, GIP from K cells) amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion after oral intake; GLP-1 agonists mimic it.
Wrong. Causes glucosuria.
cl: plasma glucose concentrations are identical in both conditions
Isolates the effect of the route of glucose delivery.
either orally or as an intravenous infusion
Only oral glucose triggers gut hormone release.
Normal β cells, so the difference reflects physiology, not disease.
q.ch: Same plasma glucose, more insulin after oral intake → gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) potentiate β-cell response → GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors exploit this.
q.tr: "Incretins = INtestine inCREases INsulin."
q.q2: The difference between the curves is mainly due to hormones that are mimicked or prolonged by which drug?
q.fc: Plasma insulin after oral vs intravenous glucose

q.s: A 9-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds) is brought in with vomiting and lethargy. Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. Her laboratory results are shown.
e: Wrong. Virilization without adrenal crisis.
Correct. Salt-wasting CAH: ↓ aldosterone and cortisol (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, hypoglycemia), ↑ 17-hydroxyprogesterone, ↑ renin and androgen excess virilizing a 46,XX infant.
Wrong. Causes hypertension with low renin.
Wrong. Causes hypertension and lack of sex steroids (no virilization).
Wrong. Affects 46,XY genital development.
Wrong. All steroids low; no virilization.
cl: ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds)
Prenatal androgen excess in a 46,XX infant.
Adrenal crisis in the second week of life.
q.ch: Virilized XX + salt wasting + hyperkalemia + high 17-OHP + high renin → 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
q.tr: "Ends in 1 (21, 11) virilizes; starts with 1 (17, 11) is hypertensive"; 21 is the salt waster.
q.q2: Which enzyme is deficient?

q.s: A 27-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has palpitations, tremor and weight loss despite good appetite. She has a diffuse nontender goiter with a bruit and mild proptosis. TSH is undetectable, free T4 is elevated and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is positive.
e: Wrong. Surgery, if needed, is done in the second trimester.
Wrong. Contraindicated in pregnancy (destroys the fetal thyroid).
Correct. PTU is preferred in the first trimester; switch to methimazole in the second and third trimesters because of PTU hepatotoxicity.
Wrong. Not a long-term therapy; can cause fetal goiter.
Wrong. She is hyperthyroid.
Wrong. Teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, embryopathy).
cl: diffuse nontender goiter with a bruit and mild proptosis
q.ch: Graves disease in the first trimester → methimazole teratogenic → PTU now → methimazole after the first trimester.
q.tr: "PTU for the Primary (first) trimester."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate antithyroid treatment at this stage of pregnancy?

q.s: A 44-year-old woman with poorly controlled Graves disease undergoes emergency appendectomy. Six hours after surgery, she is agitated and confused. Temperature is 40.6°C, pulse 168/min and irregular, and blood pressure 150/60 mm Hg. She has profuse sweating and diarrhea.
e: Wrong. She is thyrotoxic.
Wrong. Not for acute storm.
Wrong. Salicylates displace thyroid hormone from TBG and raise free hormone.
Wrong. Treats malignant hyperthermia.
Wrong. Given only after a thionamide (at least 1 hour) to avoid fueling hormone synthesis.
Correct. In thyroid storm, β-blockade controls the life-threatening tachyarrhythmia and adrenergic symptoms, and also reduces T4→T3 conversion; PTU, glucocorticoids and then iodide follow.
q.ch: Undertreated Graves + surgery → thyroid storm → β-blocker first (rate, adrenergic symptoms) → PTU → glucocorticoids → iodide.
q.tr: 4 P's in order of urgency: Propranolol, PTU, Prednisolone, Potassium iodide.
q.q2: Which drug should be given first to control the most immediately dangerous feature?

q.s: A 62-year-old woman has had hypothyroidism from Hashimoto thyroiditis for 20 years. Over 6 weeks, she has noticed a rapidly enlarging, firm, painless neck mass with hoarseness and night sweats. Fine-needle aspiration shows a monotonous population of large atypical lymphoid cells that are CD20-positive.
o: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the thyroid
e: Correct. Chronic Hashimoto thyroiditis increases the risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
Wrong. Fibrosis with few lymphocytes.
Wrong. Pleomorphic epithelial cells, not CD20-positive lymphoid cells.
Wrong. Calcitonin-producing C cells.
Wrong. Oncocytic follicular cells.
Wrong. Orphan Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies.
cl: rapidly enlarging, firm, painless neck mass
q.ch: Long-standing Hashimoto → chronic B-cell stimulation → primary thyroid lymphoma (DLBCL) → rapidly growing mass with B symptoms.
q.tr: "Hashimoto's lymphocytes can turn into Lymphoma."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 39-year-old woman has had severe anterior neck pain radiating to her jaw and ears for 10 days, with palpitations and sweating. Three weeks ago, she had an upper respiratory infection. The thyroid is exquisitely tender. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. ESR is 88 mm/h. The 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake is 2%.
e: Wrong. Not indicated.
Wrong. Uptake is low and the disease is self-limited.
Wrong. Thionamides do not help; there is no increased synthesis.
Correct. Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis releases preformed hormone; treat pain with NSAIDs (steroids if severe) and adrenergic symptoms with β-blockers.
Wrong. She is currently thyrotoxic.
Wrong. Not a bacterial infection.
cl: severe anterior neck pain radiating to her jaw and ears
Three weeks ago, she had an upper respiratory infection
Hormone leaks from damaged follicles; synthesis is shut off.
q.ch: Post-viral painful thyroid + thyrotoxicosis + high ESR + low uptake → de Quervain thyroiditis → NSAIDs + β-blocker; self-limited.
q.tr: "de QUERvain = QUite painful"; low uptake means the gland is leaking, not making.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman had radiation to the neck for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 12. She now has a 2-cm thyroid nodule and a firm 1.5-cm lymph node in the ipsilateral neck. TSH is normal. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule shows papillae lined by cells with overlapping, optically clear nuclei, intranuclear inclusions and nuclear grooves, with scattered concentric calcifications.
o: Direct invasion of the trachea in weeks
Lymphatic spread to cervical lymph nodes
e: Wrong. Anaplastic carcinoma.
Correct. Papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common type (risk ↑ with childhood irradiation), spreads via lymphatics but has a good prognosis.
Wrong. Not relevant.
Wrong. Typical of follicular carcinoma.
Wrong. Not typical.
Wrong. Ovarian cancer.
cl: radiation to the neck for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 12
firm 1.5-cm lymph node in the ipsilateral neck
q.ch: Childhood neck radiation + nodule + cervical node + Orphan Annie nuclei, grooves, psammoma bodies → papillary carcinoma → lymphatic spread.
q.tr: "Papillary = Popular, Palpable nodes, Psammoma, Prognosis good."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely route of spread of this tumor?

q.s: A 47-year-old man has a 3-cm firm thyroid nodule and diarrhea for 3 months. Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are elevated. He has no family history of endocrine tumors. A plasma metanephrine test is ordered before surgery.
o: Uniform follicles invading the capsule and vessels
Sheets of polygonal cells in a stroma that is Congo red–positive
e: Wrong. Subacute thyroiditis.
Wrong. Anaplastic carcinoma.
Wrong. Follicular carcinoma.
Wrong. Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Wrong. Papillary carcinoma.
Correct. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, secretes calcitonin (diarrhea can occur) and has amyloid stroma; pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery.
cl: Calcitonin and other tumor peptides can cause diarrhea.
Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are elevated
A plasma metanephrine test is ordered before surgery
q.ch: Thyroid nodule + high calcitonin + diarrhea → medullary carcinoma (C cells) → amyloid stroma; check for pheochromocytoma before surgery.
q.tr: "MEDULLARY = Makes calcitonin, Amyloid, MEN2."
q.q2: The thyroid biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman has a 2.5-cm thyroid nodule found on examination. She has mild palpitations. TSH is 0.05 µU/mL (suppressed) and free T4 is at the upper limit of normal.
o: CT of the neck with contrast
e: Wrong. Needs evaluation now.
Wrong. Iodinated contrast interferes with scanning.
Correct. A low TSH suggests a hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule; scintigraphy confirms it, and hot nodules are rarely malignant.
Wrong. With a suppressed TSH, a scan comes first; a hot nodule is rarely malignant and does not need biopsy.
Wrong. Not routine first step.
Wrong. Not the first step.
cl: Subclinical hyperthyroidism from an autonomous nodule.
q.ch: Thyroid nodule + low TSH → radionuclide scan → hot (benign, treat hyperthyroidism) vs cold (biopsy); normal or high TSH → ultrasound and FNA.
q.tr: "Low TSH → Look with a scan; normal TSH → Needle (FNA)."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

q.s: A 79-year-old woman is found confused at home in winter. She stopped taking her thyroid pills months ago. Temperature is 33.1°C, pulse 44/min and respirations 8/min. She has periorbital puffiness, nonpitting edema and delayed reflexes. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L and glucose is 58 mg/dL. TSH is 96 µU/mL.
o: Oral levothyroxine alone at a low dose
Hypertonic saline and fluid restriction only
Rapid external rewarming with hot blankets alone
e: Correct. Myxedema coma needs IV thyroid hormone; stress-dose glucocorticoids are given first or simultaneously because adrenal insufficiency may coexist and thyroid hormone raises cortisol clearance.
Wrong. Too slow; IV therapy is needed in coma.
Wrong. She is hypothyroid.
Wrong. Not reliable in coma.
Wrong. Does not treat the cause.
Wrong. Risks vasodilatory collapse and does not treat the cause.
cl: stopped taking her thyroid pills months ago
q.ch: Untreated hypothyroidism + cold stress → myxedema coma → IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone + supportive care.
q.tr: Myxedema coma: "Steroids before (or with) Thyroid."
q.q2: In addition to supportive care, which treatment combination is most appropriate?

q.s: A 66-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 2 years for ventricular tachycardia. He now has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation. TSH is 18 µU/mL and free T4 is low.
o: It contains a large amount of iodine, which can inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis
It causes antibodies against the TSH receptor
e: Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Wrong. Amiodarone has β-blocking activity.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Correct. The iodine load triggers the Wolff-Chaikoff effect (hypothyroidism) in susceptible glands, and amiodarone also inhibits peripheral deiodination; it can also cause thyrotoxicosis.
Wrong. That is Graves disease.
Wrong. TSH is high, so the pituitary works.
cl: TSH is 18 µU/mL and free T4 is low
fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation
q.ch: Amiodarone (≈37% iodine by weight) → iodine excess → Wolff-Chaikoff effect + ↓ deiodinase → primary hypothyroidism (or thyrotoxicosis in other patients).
q.tr: Amiodarone is an "iodine pill": too much iodine can turn the thyroid Off (Wolff) or On (Jod-Basedow).
q.q2: Which property of amiodarone best explains this complication?

q.s: A 38-year-old man has had headaches, decreased libido and erectile dysfunction for a year. He bumps into door frames on both sides. Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia. Serum prolactin is 1,850 ng/mL (normal <17). MRI shows a 3.2-cm sellar mass extending to the optic chiasm.
o: Transsphenoidal surgery as the first step in all cases
e: Wrong. Does not treat the tumor.
Wrong. Medical therapy is first-line even for large prolactinomas with visual loss.
Wrong. Not first line.
Wrong. Used for GH- and TSH-secreting tumors.
Correct. Dopamine agonists shrink prolactinomas, lower prolactin and often restore vision.
Wrong. A dopamine antagonist raises prolactin.
cl: Very high levels mean a prolactinoma (not stalk compression).
q.ch: Macroadenoma + very high prolactin + hypogonadism + chiasm compression → prolactinoma → dopamine agonist (cabergoline) first.
q.tr: "Prolactinoma? Pills before Scalpel" (cabergoline, bromocriptine).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

q.s: A 51-year-old man has numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers of both hands, worse at night. Over several years his shoe size has increased, his teeth have spread apart and he snores loudly. Blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg. Fasting glucose is 138 mg/dL.
o: Failure of growth hormone to suppress below threshold after a 75-g oral glucose load
Elevated morning cortisol that suppresses with dexamethasone
e: Correct. Acromegaly is screened with IGF-1 and confirmed by lack of GH suppression after oral glucose.
Wrong. Confirms carpal tunnel, not the cause.
Wrong. Hypothyroidism can cause carpal tunnel but not the other features.
Wrong. A normal response.
Wrong. Prolactinoma.
Wrong. IGF-1 is high in acromegaly.
cl: numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers of both hands
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (soft tissue overgrowth).
his shoe size has increased, his teeth have spread apart
q.ch: Acral enlargement + jaw growth + carpal tunnel + sleep apnea + hypertension + hyperglycemia → acromegaly → ↑ IGF-1, no GH suppression after OGTT.
q.tr: Acromegaly: "rings, shoes and hats get tight."
q.q2: Which test result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 47-year-old woman with a known 2-cm nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma suddenly develops the worst headache of her life, vomiting and double vision. Examination shows bilateral visual field loss and a right third nerve palsy. Blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg. MRI shows hemorrhage within the adenoma.
e: Wrong. Not the treatment.
Wrong. DI is less common and not the immediate threat.
Wrong. Not a migraine.
Wrong. Not for a nonfunctioning hemorrhagic adenoma.
Wrong. Giving thyroid hormone before steroids can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Correct. Pituitary apoplexy causes acute ACTH deficiency (hypotension); stress-dose glucocorticoids are lifesaving, followed by surgical decompression if vision is threatened.
cl: worst headache of her life, vomiting and double vision
Sudden expansion compressing the cavernous sinus.
q.ch: Hemorrhage into an adenoma → sudden pituitary failure (ACTH loss → shock) + compression → IV glucocorticoids, then decompression.
q.tr: Apoplexy: "Steroids first, Surgeon second."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most urgent treatment?

q.s: A 33-year-old woman delivered 6 months ago, with massive hemorrhage requiring 8 units of blood. She could not breastfeed and her periods have not returned. She has fatigue, cold intolerance and dizziness on standing. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L and potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. Morning cortisol is low, ACTH is inappropriately normal, free T4 is low and TSH is low-normal.
o: Her kidneys retain potassium less in the postpartum period
Aldosterone secretion is preserved because it is regulated mainly by the renin-angiotensin system
Her ACTH is high, stimulating aldosterone
e: Wrong. Transfusion tends to raise K+.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Wrong. ACTH would be high, with hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia.
Wrong. Not the explanation.
Correct. In secondary adrenal insufficiency (Sheehan syndrome), the glomerulosa is intact, so there is no hyperkalemia; hyponatremia comes from cortisol deficiency (↑ ADH).
Wrong. ACTH is not high.
q.k: Sheehan syndrome and secondary adrenal insufficiency
cl: massive hemorrhage requiring 8 units of blood
Postpartum hypotension infarcting the enlarged pituitary.
She could not breastfeed and her periods have not returned
q.ch: Postpartum hemorrhage → pituitary infarction → ↓ ACTH, TSH, PRL, LH/FSH → low cortisol (hyponatremia) but RAAS-driven aldosterone intact → normal K+.
q.tr: "Secondary adrenal insufficiency: no Salt crisis, no Skin color (no hyperkalemia, no hyperpigmentation)."
q.q2: Why is her potassium normal despite adrenal insufficiency?

q.s: A 67-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has confusion. Serum sodium is 114 mEq/L, serum osmolality 238 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 610 mOsm/kg. He is euvolemic. He receives hypertonic saline, and his sodium rises to 131 mEq/L over the next 24 hours. Two days later he develops dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis.
o: Brain metastases from the lung cancer
Osmotic demyelination of the central pons from overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia
e: Wrong. The timing after rapid correction is classic for another cause.
Wrong. Cerebral edema results from too-rapid lowering of osmolality, not raising.
Correct. Raising sodium too quickly (here 17 mEq/L in 24 h) causes osmotic demyelination syndrome; correction should be limited to about 8–10 mEq/L per day.
Wrong. Proximal weakness improving with use, not acute bulbar quadriparesis.
Wrong. Not consistent.
Wrong. Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion.
cl: sodium rises to 131 mEq/L over the next 24 hours
17 mEq/L in a day: too fast.
q.ch: SIADH with chronic hyponatremia → brain cells adapt by losing osmolytes → rapid Na+ rise shrinks cells → pontine demyelination.
q.tr: "From low to high, your pons will die; from high to low, your brain will blow."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his new neurologic findings?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman took prednisone 40 mg daily for 9 months for polymyalgia rheumatica and stopped it abruptly 4 days ago because of weight gain. She now has severe fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain and dizziness. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 131 mEq/L and potassium is 4.4 mEq/L. Her skin is not hyperpigmented.
o: Bilateral atrophy of the zona fasciculata and reticularis from chronic ACTH suppression
Autoimmune destruction of all three zones
e: Wrong. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
Correct. Long-term glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy; abrupt withdrawal causes tertiary adrenal insufficiency (crisis without hyperkalemia).
Wrong. Tuberculous Addison disease.
Wrong. ACTH was suppressed by prednisone.
Wrong. Primary (Addison) disease would cause hyperkalemia and pigmentation.
Wrong. Not related.
q.k: Tertiary adrenal insufficiency from steroid withdrawal
q.ch: Chronic exogenous steroids → ↓ CRH/ACTH → atrophy of fasciculata/reticularis → abrupt stop → adrenal crisis without hyperkalemia or pigmentation → stress-dose steroids, slow taper.
q.tr: "Tertiary from Treatment": taper, never Terminate.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes her adrenal glands?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo has had fatigue, weight loss, salt craving and lightheadedness for 3 months. Her insulin requirements have fallen and she has had several hypoglycemic episodes. Her buccal mucosa and palmar creases are darkened. Sodium is 128 mEq/L and potassium 5.9 mEq/L. TSH is 9.8 µU/mL.
o: Autoimmune adrenalitis as part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2
e: Wrong. Presents in childhood.
Wrong. Most common cause in low-income countries; her autoimmune history points elsewhere.
Wrong. Unlikely at her age.
Correct. Addison disease with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease (Schmidt syndrome); falling insulin needs reflect cortisol deficiency.
Wrong. Would cause secondary insufficiency without hyperkalemia.
Wrong. Would not cause hyperkalemia or pigmentation.
cl: buccal mucosa and palmar creases are darkened
q.ch: Autoimmune background + hyperpigmentation + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + falling insulin needs + hypothyroidism → primary autoimmune adrenalitis in polyglandular syndrome type 2.
q.tr: Polyglandular type 2 = "Adrenal + Thyroid + Type 1 diabetes."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her adrenal disease?

q.s: A 4-year-old unvaccinated boy has fever for 12 hours, then a rapidly spreading petechial and purpuric rash. He is hypotensive and unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors. He dies within hours. Cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative diplococci.
e: Wrong. Tuberculosis.
Correct. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: acute bilateral adrenal hemorrhage in meningococcemia (DIC, endotoxin), causing acute adrenal failure and shock.
Wrong. Not related.
Wrong. Not consistent.
Wrong. ACTH excess.
Wrong. Steroid suppression.
cl: rapidly spreading petechial and purpuric rash
Adrenal crisis contributes to refractory shock.
q.ch: Meningococcemia → endotoxin, DIC → bilateral adrenal hemorrhage → acute primary adrenal insufficiency → refractory shock.
q.tr: Waterhouse-Friderichsen = "Wide-spread purpura + Failure of adrenals."
q.q2: Autopsy would most likely show which of the following in the adrenal glands?

q.s: A 46-year-old man has hypertension that remains uncontrolled on three drugs, including a diuretic. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. He has no edema. The plasma aldosterone concentration is high and plasma renin activity is suppressed. CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule.
e: Wrong. For renovascular hypertension (renin would be high).
Wrong. For Cushing syndrome.
Wrong. Tests for pheochromocytoma.
Wrong. For adrenal insufficiency.
Correct. Lateralization of aldosterone secretion confirms a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) rather than bilateral hyperplasia with an incidental nodule.
Wrong. For Cushing syndrome.
cl: uncontrolled on three drugs, including a diuretic
Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L
q.ch: Resistant hypertension + hypokalemic alkalosis + high aldosterone with low renin → primary hyperaldosteronism → adrenal vein sampling to lateralize → adrenalectomy (or spironolactone/eplerenone for bilateral disease).
q.tr: Conn: "Can't control BP, K+ low, renin low."
q.q2: Before surgery, which test best confirms that the nodule is the source of excess hormone?

q.s: A 40-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor lasting 15 minutes, several times a week. Blood pressure during an episode is 220/120 mm Hg; between episodes it is 138/88 mm Hg. Her fasting glucose is 128 mg/dL and hematocrit is 52%.
o: CT of the abdomen before any blood test
e: Correct. Pheochromocytoma is screened with plasma free (or 24-hour urine fractionated) metanephrines; then imaging localizes the tumor.
Wrong. For Cushing syndrome.
Wrong. For medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Wrong. For carcinoid syndrome.
Wrong. Biochemical confirmation comes before imaging.
Wrong. Hyperthyroidism lacks paroxysms of severe hypertension with pallor.
cl: pounding headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor
q.ch: Paroxysms of pressure, pain, perspiration, palpitations, pallor + polycythemia + hyperglycemia → pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines first, then imaging.
q.tr: Pheo's 5 P's; test the "Products" (metanephrines) before the "Picture" (CT).
q.q2: Which of the following is the best initial diagnostic test?

q.s: A 2-year-old girl has a firm, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline. She also has periorbital bruising ("raccoon eyes") and rapid, chaotic eye movements with jerking of her limbs. Blood pressure is normal. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated.
e: Wrong. Retinoblastoma.
Wrong. Small cell lung cancer.
Wrong. Burkitt lymphoma (translocation).
Correct. Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain; N-myc amplification predicts aggressive disease.
Wrong. Wilms tumor (smooth, does not cross the midline).
Wrong. MEN2.
cl: rapid, chaotic eye movements with jerking of her limbs
homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated
q.ch: Toddler + irregular abdominal mass crossing midline + raccoon eyes + opsoclonus-myoclonus + ↑ HVA/VMA → neuroblastoma → N-myc amplification = poor prognosis.
q.tr: "N-myc for Neuroblastoma"; "dancing eyes, dancing feet."
q.q2: Amplification of which gene is associated with a poor prognosis in this tumor?

q.s: A 17-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep rapid breathing after missing insulin doses during a viral illness. Glucose is 540 mg/dL, pH 7.10, bicarbonate 7 mEq/L, anion gap 28, and serum ketones are strongly positive. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L.
o: Start an IV insulin infusion immediately
e: Wrong. Not routinely indicated at pH 7.10; worsens hypokalemia.
Wrong. DKA needs IV regular insulin after K+ is safe.
Correct. Despite acidosis, her total body potassium is severely depleted; when K+ is <3.3 mEq/L, insulin is held until potassium is replaced.
Wrong. Added later when glucose falls to ~200–250 mg/dL.
Wrong. For hyperkalemia.
Wrong. Insulin will drive potassium further into cells and can cause fatal hypokalemia.
cl: missing insulin doses during a viral illness
Low serum K+ despite acidosis means profound total body depletion.
q.ch: DKA → osmotic diuresis drains total body K+ → serum K+ already low → insulin would shift more K+ into cells → replete K+ first (insulin when K+ ≥3.3).
q.tr: DKA order: "Fluids, Find the K+, then insulin" — no insulin if K+ <3.3.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step after starting IV fluids?

q.s: An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes in a nursing home has had increasing lethargy for 4 days after developing a urinary tract infection. She has been drinking poorly. She is obtunded with dry mucous membranes and a left-sided weakness. Glucose is 1,120 mg/dL, serum osmolality 372 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L and serum ketones trace.
o: Ketones are excreted rapidly by the kidneys
Her liver cannot synthesize ketone bodies
Residual insulin secretion suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis but not hyperglycemia
e: Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Wrong. Not the explanation.
Wrong. Hepatic ketogenesis is intact.
Wrong. Not the explanation.
Wrong. Glucagon promotes ketogenesis.
Correct. In hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, low insulin levels are still enough to inhibit lipolysis, so the illness is dominated by severe dehydration and hyperosmolality.
cl: type 2 diabetes in a nursing home
Older patient with limited access to water.
Focal neurologic deficits occur in HHS.
q.ch: Older T2DM + infection + poor intake → profound hyperglycemia → osmotic diuresis → severe dehydration and hyperosmolality; residual insulin prevents ketosis → HHS.
q.tr: HHS: "Hyperosmolar, Hydration-depleted, Hardly any ketones."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the absence of significant ketoacidosis?

q.s: A 36-year-old woman has episodes of confusion, sweating and blurred vision in the late morning, relieved by eating. She has gained 9 kg. During a supervised 72-hour fast, she becomes symptomatic with glucose 38 mg/dL; symptoms resolve with IV dextrose. At that time, insulin and C-peptide are elevated, proinsulin is elevated and a sulfonylurea screen is negative.
e: Correct. Whipple triad with inappropriately high insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin and a negative drug screen indicates a β-cell tumor.
Wrong. C-peptide would be low.
Wrong. Occurs after meals, not during fasting.
Wrong. Causes hyperglycemia.
Wrong. The screen is negative.
Wrong. Insulin would be suppressed.
cl: insulin and C-peptide are elevated, proinsulin is elevated
q.ch: Fasting hypoglycemia + Whipple triad + high insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin + negative sulfonylurea screen → insulinoma.
q.tr: "C-peptide high: the body made it (tumor or sulfonylurea); C-peptide low: a needle put it in."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman whose husband has type 2 diabetes is brought in after being found confused with glucose 34 mg/dL. She has no diabetes. Insulin and C-peptide levels are both elevated. Proinsulin is elevated. Imaging of the pancreas is normal.
o: Plasma screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides
e: Wrong. Insulin autoimmune syndrome is rare.
Wrong. Not indicated.
Wrong. Pancreatic imaging is normal; check drugs first.
Correct. Secretagogues raise endogenous insulin and C-peptide just like an insulinoma; access to her husband's medication makes surreptitious use likely.
Wrong. Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia has low insulin.
Wrong. Not indicated with high insulin.
cl: Insulin and C-peptide levels are both elevated
Imaging of the pancreas is normal
q.ch: Hypoglycemia + high insulin and C-peptide + access to diabetes pills + normal imaging → secretagogue ingestion → sulfonylurea screen.
q.tr: Sulfonylureas "Sneak up" like insulinomas: both raise C-peptide; only the drug screen tells them apart.
q.q2: Which of the following tests is most likely to reveal the cause?

q.s: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease takes metformin. He undergoes a CT angiogram with iodinated contrast for chest pain. Two days later, he has vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid breathing. Arterial pH is 7.08, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, anion gap 30 and lactate 11 mmol/L. Creatinine has risen from 1.8 to 3.6 mg/dL.
o: Metformin accumulation from contrast-induced kidney injury inhibiting hepatic lactate clearance
e: Wrong. Not the cause of acidosis.
Wrong. No history.
Correct. Metformin is renally cleared; acute kidney injury causes accumulation, and metformin inhibits mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and gluconeogenesis, impairing lactate use.
Wrong. Lactate of 11 is far beyond uremia.
Wrong. No history.
Wrong. Ketones are not mentioned and lactate is very high.
cl: stage 3 chronic kidney disease takes metformin
Creatinine has risen from 1.8 to 3.6 mg/dL
q.ch: Metformin + CKD + contrast AKI → metformin accumulates → ↓ hepatic lactate uptake (↓ gluconeogenesis) → lactic acidosis.
q.tr: Metformin: hold for "Contrast, Creatinine rising, Cirrhosis, Critical illness."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the acidosis?

q.s: A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and empagliflozin. She had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 2 days ago and has been eating little. She now has nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Glucose is 178 mg/dL, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, anion gap 25 and serum β-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated. Lactate is normal.
o: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis associated with SGLT2 inhibition
e: Wrong. Does not explain ketoacidosis.
Wrong. No alcohol history.
Wrong. Glucose is not very high and there is acidosis.
Wrong. Does not cause such severe acidosis.
Correct. SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose through glucosuria and favor ketogenesis (↓ insulin, ↑ glucagon); with fasting or surgery, DKA can occur with near-normal glucose.
Wrong. Lactate is normal.
cl: Reduced carbohydrate intake and insulin need.
q.ch: SGLT2 inhibitor + surgery/fasting → glucosuria keeps glucose modest while low insulin and high glucagon drive ketogenesis → euglycemic DKA.
q.tr: "Gliflozins let sugar Flow out — and ketones can sneak in with normal sugar."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her condition?

q.s: A 10-year-old boy has had polyuria, polydipsia and a 4-kg weight loss over 3 weeks. Random glucose is 410 mg/dL and urine ketones are positive. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase are positive. His identical twin brother is healthy.
o: T-cell–mediated autoimmune destruction of β cells, associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4
Insulin resistance with islet amyloid deposition
e: Wrong. Hemochromatosis.
Correct. Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune insulitis; twin concordance is only about 50%, showing environmental factors matter.
Wrong. Type 2 diabetes.
Wrong. Not at this age with autoantibodies.
Wrong. Secondary diabetes.
Wrong. A form of MODY; ketoacidosis and autoantibodies are not typical.
cl: polyuria, polydipsia and a 4-kg weight loss
Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase are positive
His identical twin brother is healthy
q.ch: Child + rapid onset + ketonuria + anti-GAD → type 1 diabetes → T-cell destruction of β cells (HLA-DR3/DR4); incomplete twin concordance.
q.tr: "4 − 3 = 1": HLA-DR4 and DR3 for type 1.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of his disease?

q.s: A 58-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 15 years and diabetic retinopathy. Blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 420 mg/g. A renal biopsy shows thickened glomerular basement membranes and round, acellular eosinophilic nodules in the mesangium.
e: Wrong. Less proven.
Wrong. Not renoprotective.
Wrong. Do not slow nephropathy.
Wrong. Harmful to the kidney.
Wrong. Glucose control helps, but sulfonylureas do not specifically protect the kidney.
Correct. Diabetic nephropathy (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) is slowed by RAAS blockade, which lowers glomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole; SGLT2 inhibitors add benefit.
cl: round, acellular eosinophilic nodules in the mesangium
q.ch: Long-standing diabetes → nonenzymatic glycation, hyperfiltration → GBM thickening and nodular glomerulosclerosis → albuminuria → ACE inhibitor/ARB lowers intraglomerular pressure.
q.tr: ACE inhibitors "Ease" the efferent arteriole and protect diabetic kidneys.
q.q2: Which drug class best slows progression of his kidney disease?

q.s: A 61-year-old man has episodes of facial flushing, watery diarrhea and wheezing. He has hepatomegaly with multiple liver masses. Echocardiography shows thickened tricuspid and pulmonic valves. He also has a scaly, sun-exposed dermatitis and memory problems.
o: Diversion of tryptophan into serotonin synthesis, causing niacin deficiency
e: Correct. Carcinoid syndrome consumes tryptophan, the precursor for niacin, causing pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).
Wrong. Not typical.
Wrong. Does not cause pellagra.
Wrong. Contributes to flushing but not pellagra.
Wrong. Not the cause of photosensitive dermatitis.
Wrong. Acrodermatitis, not this picture.
cl: facial flushing, watery diarrhea and wheezing
Liver metastases bypass first-pass serotonin metabolism.
scaly, sun-exposed dermatitis and memory problems
q.ch: Carcinoid with liver metastases → systemic serotonin → flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, right-sided valve disease; tryptophan diverted to serotonin → niacin deficiency → pellagra.
q.tr: Pellagra's 3 D's (Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia) — carcinoid "steals Tryptophan."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his skin and memory findings?

q.s: A 45-year-old man has refractory peptic ulcers in the duodenum and jejunum despite high-dose omeprazole, plus chronic diarrhea with greasy stools. Fasting serum gastrin is 1,100 pg/mL while off PPIs, and gastric pH is 1.2. After intravenous secretin, gastrin rises further. His brother had a parathyroid adenoma.
o: Bile acid malabsorption from ileal disease
Acid inactivation of pancreatic enzymes in the small bowel
e: Wrong. He has hyperchlorhydria.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Wrong. Somatostatinoma causes achlorhydria.
Wrong. Not consistent.
Wrong. Not consistent.
Correct. Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) floods the duodenum with acid, inactivating lipase and damaging mucosa; family history suggests MEN1.
cl: refractory peptic ulcers in the duodenum and jejunum
After intravenous secretin, gastrin rises further
His brother had a parathyroid adenoma
q.ch: Refractory distal ulcers + high gastrin with low pH + positive secretin test → gastrinoma → acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes → steatorrhea; family parathyroid disease → MEN1.
q.tr: ZES: "Secretin Stimulates the gastrinoma" (normally secretin suppresses gastrin).
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his diarrhea and steatorrhea?

q.s: A 41-year-old woman has panhypopituitarism after surgery for a large pituitary adenoma. She is started on hormone replacement. Two days after beginning levothyroxine alone, she develops weakness, vomiting and hypotension.
o: Thyroid hormone increased cortisol metabolism and requirements, unmasking untreated adrenal insufficiency
Thyroid storm from an excessive dose
e: Wrong. Not a drug effect.
Wrong. GH is deficient.
Correct. In hypopituitarism, glucocorticoids must be replaced before (or with) thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis.
Wrong. Not consistent.
Wrong. Aldosterone is preserved in pituitary disease.
Wrong. Not with a standard replacement dose.
cl: Deficiency of ACTH and TSH (among others).
q.ch: Panhypopituitarism → ACTH and TSH deficient → thyroxine alone raises metabolic rate and cortisol clearance → adrenal crisis → always replace glucocorticoids first.
q.tr: "Cortisol before Thyroxine — C comes before T."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her deterioration?

q.s: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin glargine and glipizide has hypertension and stable angina. His physician recently started a nonselective β-blocker. His wife finds him confused and sweaty one afternoon; glucose is 36 mg/dL. He says he had no warning shakiness, palpitations or hunger before the episode, unlike previous episodes.
o: β-blockade blunted the adrenergic (neurogenic) symptoms of hypoglycemia
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy is the only possible cause
e: Wrong. Not the explanation.

Correct. Tremor, palpitations and anxiety are β-adrenergic; blocking them causes hypoglycemia unawareness (sweating, being cholinergic, may persist). Nonselective β-blockers can also delay recovery by blocking glycogenolysis.
Wrong. Glargine is peakless.
Wrong. Possible, but the new β-blocker is the clear precipitant.
Wrong. β2 blockade tends to reduce insulin release.
Wrong. Not correct.
cl: no warning shakiness, palpitations or hunger
q.ch: Insulin/sulfonylurea hypoglycemia + new nonselective β-blocker → blocked tremor and tachycardia → neuroglycopenia without warning (sweating may remain).
q.tr: "β-blockers Blind you to lows" — sweating is the symptom that survives (cholinergic).
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the absence of warning symptoms?
